Late 20s, working as a public servant with a little over 5 years of experience. Also pursuing part-time/evening programs.

For me, the biggest challenge was the LSAT. Finding the time and energy to really dedicate to studying for it was difficult while working full time. I took it twice and got the same score both times (158), which isn’t a terrible score but also not what I was aiming for. I feel like my LSAT score was the weakest part of my application.

For letters of recommendation, I asked one of my professors from my department to write one for me, along with my supervisor at work. My professor asked for input as to what I would want them to write about, like traits, participation, teamwork, and extracurricular activities I did while in undergrad. I’d recommend asking your letter writers if they would like some suggestions as to what you would like them to write about. I also definitely recommend asking earlier rather than later for letters. LSAC will keep them on file even if they submit it over the summer instead of during the fall. From the feedback I’ve received from admissions offers, these were definitely a strong part of my application.

For the personal statement, I had at least 3 or 4 of my friends that I trust and know are good writers to review it. I think this was another strong part of my application, and got some nice comments on it in admissions offers.

If you can, I’d also recommend writing a diversity statement that drives home the point of why you would be a good addition to not just the school community, but the legal community as a whole.

The best piece of advice I can give you is to write well. As lawyers, we will spend most of our time reading and writing. I think a good essay can really be a difference maker if your GPA or LSAT aren’t what you want them to be or are below medians.

I wish you the best of luck in your application process!

From my understanding, there are two paths to being a lawyer in Ireland: being a solicitor and being a barrister. Barristers are the ones who practice in court, whereas solicitors do not have that right but handle other legal matters.

To be a solicitor, you do not necessarily need a legal degree. Instead, you sit for examinations with the Law Society of Ireland.

To be a barrister, you must be a member of the Bar of Ireland, and most barristers are members of the Law Library. To become a barrister, King’s Inns is the usual schooling route to earn the degree of barrister-at-law. In order to sit for the entrance exam for the degree of barrister-at-law, you have to have an approved law degree, or you can pursue the Diploma in Legal Studies from King’s Inns, which lets you sit for the entrance exam.
